directAnswer: Pope Alexander VI was Rodrigo de Borja (Borgia), a Valencian-born cardinal and nephew of Callixtus III, who reigned from 1492 to 1503. He issued the bull Inter caetera dividing newly explored lands between Spain and Portugal, and his openly acknowledged children, including Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia, made his pontificate one of the most controversial of the Renaissance.

sections.h2: Rodrigo Borgia, Vice-Chancellor of the Church
paras: Rodrigo de Borja was born around 1431 at Xativa in the Kingdom of Valencia, part of the Crown of Aragon. His uncle Alfonso de Borja became Pope Callixtus III in 1455 and made Rodrigo a cardinal the following year, then vice-chancellor of the Church, an office he held for some 35 years under five popes.

He was an able administrator and immensely wealthy. He also fathered several children, most notably Cesare, Juan, Lucrezia and Jofre by Vannozza dei Cattanei. In August 1492 he was elected pope; contemporaries alleged that votes had been bought, a charge many historians consider likely.

sections.h2: Inter Caetera and the New World
paras: Months after Columbus returned from his first voyage, Alexander VI issued a series of bulls in 1493, chief among them Inter caetera, that drew a line in the Atlantic and assigned lands beyond it to Castile, with the duty of evangelizing their peoples. Spain and Portugal adjusted the line themselves in the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494.

In 1496 he granted Ferdinand and Isabella the title of Catholic Monarchs. These decisions shaped the colonial map of the Americas for centuries and remain a subject of debate in discussions of conquest and missionary history.

In 1494 King Charles VIII of France invaded Italy to claim Naples and entered Rome, forcing the pope to negotiate from Castel Sant'Angelo. Alexander VI then helped organize the League of Venice that pushed the French out.

In Florence the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola denounced corruption in the Church and the papacy. Alexander VI ordered him to stop preaching and excommunicated him in 1497. In 1498 Florentine authorities tried and executed Savonarola, an episode that remains part of the pope's contested legacy.

sections.h2: Cesare Borgia and the Papal States
paras: After the murder of his son Juan in 1497, which was never solved, Alexander VI spoke of reforming his life and the Curia, but the plans faded. Instead he backed Cesare, who renounced the cardinalate and led campaigns to subdue the lords of the Romagna, building a Borgia power base within the Papal States.

Alexander VI celebrated the Jubilee of 1500 and commissioned Pinturicchio to decorate the Borgia Apartments in the Vatican. He died on 18 August 1503, probably of malaria. Later Catholic historians, including Ludwig von Pastor, judged his private life severely while acknowledging his political skill; the Church has never defended his conduct.

keyFacts: Born Rodrigo de Borja at Xativa, Kingdom of Valencia, around 1431
Nephew of Pope Callixtus III; vice-chancellor of the Church for decades
Issued Inter caetera (1493) on lands of the New World
Father of Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia among other children

faqs.question: What was the bull Inter caetera?
faqs.answer: A 1493 decree of Alexander VI that drew a line through the Atlantic and assigned newly found lands west of it to Castile, with a charge to evangelize. Spain and Portugal moved the line in the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas.

faqs.question: Did Pope Alexander VI have children?
faqs.answer: Yes. He acknowledged several children, the best known being Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia, born to Vannozza dei Cattanei before his election.

faqs.question: How does the Church view Alexander VI today?
faqs.answer: Catholic historians have long criticized his private life and nepotism. His case is often cited to show that the authority of the papal office does not depend on the personal holiness of the man who holds it.
